name: Plus sign
definition: Denotes addition of two numbers, or marks a number as positive. Placed between two values it combines them; placed before one value it asserts positivity.

examples.explanation: Three plus four equals seven.
Positive five.

name: Minus sign
definition: Denotes subtraction of one number from another, or marks a number as negative. The typographic minus (−) differs from the keyboard hyphen (-), though both are read the same way.

examples.explanation: Nine minus four equals five.
Negative three.

name: Multiplication sign
definition: Denotes multiplication of two numbers. A centered dot (·) or parentheses are common alternatives; in algebra the sign is usually dropped entirely.

examples.explanation: Six times seven equals forty-two.
Parentheses alone can denote multiplication.

commonMistakes: Confusing × with the letter x in handwriting; the dot or parentheses avoid this.

name: Division sign
definition: Denotes division of one number by another. Fractions and the slash are more common in algebra and beyond.

examples.explanation: Twenty divided by four equals five.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e

name: Plus-minus sign
definition: Gives two values at once: one with plus, one with minus. It commonly expresses a tolerance or lists both square roots.

examples.explanation: x equals 3 or x equals negative 3.
A measurement of 5.0 with tolerance 0.1 either way.

name: Minus-plus sign
definition: The mirror of plus-minus: it takes the opposite sign to a paired ± in the same expression, so both combinations are covered exactly once.

examples.explanation: The two signs stay in step: upper with upper, lower with lower.

name: Equals sign
definition: Asserts that the two sides have exactly the same value. An equation is a statement using this sign.

examples.explanation: The left side and the right side are the same number.

commonMistakes: Reading = as “do the next step”; it states equality, so 2 + 3 = 5 + 1 is false.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Not equal to
definition: Asserts that the two sides have different values. It is the negation of the equals sign.

examples.explanation: Four is not equal to five.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Approximately equal to
definition: States that two values are close but not exactly equal, typically after rounding or measurement.

examples.explanation: Pi rounded to two decimals is about 3.14.

commonMistakes: Using ≈ where = belongs after exact simplification.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Identically equal to
definition: A triple bar with several related uses: an identity true for all values, a definition, or congruence modulo n in number theory. The surrounding context decides.
reading: “is identically equal to” or “is congruent to”.

examples.explanation: An identity: true for every x.
17 and 5 leave the same remainder on division by 12.

contexts.meaning: An identity holding for all values of the variables.
Modular congruence: equal remainders after division.
Sometimes used for congruence of figures; ≅ is more standard.

name: Less than
definition: States that the left value is strictly smaller than the right value. The open end of the symbol faces the larger side.

examples.explanation: Three is less than seven.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Greater than
definition: States that the left value is strictly larger than the right value.

examples.explanation: Nine is greater than two.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Less than or equal to
definition: States that the left value is smaller than or equal to the right value. Includes the endpoint, unlike strict <.

examples.explanation: x is at most 5; 5 itself is allowed.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Greater than or equal to
definition: States that the left value is larger than or equal to the right value. Includes the endpoint.

examples.explanation: n is at least 1.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Fraction
definition: Writes division of a numerator by a nonzero denominator. The value is the quotient; the denominator can never be zero.

examples.explanation: Three quarters equals 0.75.

commonMistakes: Dividing by zero, which is undefined, not zero.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Decimal point
definition: Separates the whole part of a decimal number from its fractional part. Each position after the point is a further division by ten.

examples.explanation: The 5 sits in the tenths place.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Percent
definition: Means parts per hundred. x% equals x divided by 100, so it converts directly between ratios and decimals.

examples.explanation: Twenty-five percent is a quarter.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Ratio
definition: Compares two quantities by division. a:b states how many of a come with each b, keeping the same units relationship.

examples.explanation: Two parts to three parts, e.g. in a mixture.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Proportion
definition: States that two ratios are equal. Solving a proportion usually means cross-multiplying to find the unknown term.
reading: “a is to b as c is to d”.

examples.explanation: One half equals two quarters; the ratios match.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Power (exponentiation)
definition: Raises a base to an exponent: x to the n means x multiplied by itself n times. Special cases include squares, cubes, zero exponents and negative exponents.

examples.explanation: Two cubed: 2 times 2 times 2.
A negative exponent takes the reciprocal, for nonzero x.

commonMistakes: Writing 2x cubed as 2x^3 when (2x)^3 is meant; the exponent binds to x alone.

sources.label: OpenStax Elementary Algebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Square root
definition: Asks which nonnegative number squares to give x. Every positive number has two square roots, ±; the radical sign alone means the principal (nonnegative) one.

examples.explanation: Seven squared is 49, and the sign gives the positive root.

commonMistakes: Writing sqrt(49) = ±7; the ± appears when solving x^2 = 49, not from the radical alone.

sources.label: OpenStax Elementary Algebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: nth root
definition: Asks which number raised to the nth power gives x. The small index n names the root; with n = 2 it is the ordinary square root, with n = 3 the cube root.

examples.explanation: Three cubed is 27.
Roots are fractional exponents, where defined (for even n, x must be nonnegative for a real root).

sources.label: OpenStax Intermediate Algebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Absolute value
definition: Gives the distance of x from zero, always nonnegative. Vertical bars mean different operations in other contexts (determinants, cardinality, divisibility), so read the setting.

examples.explanation: Negative four is four units from zero.

contexts.meaning: Distance from zero on the number line.
Bars around a matrix mean its determinant.
Bars around a set mean its size (cardinality).

sources.label: OpenStax Elementary Algebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Factorial
definition: Multiplies all positive integers up to n. It counts orderings: n! is the number of ways to arrange n distinct objects. By convention 0! = 1.

examples.explanation: Five objects can be ordered in 120 ways.
Empty product convention: there is one way to order nothing.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 5
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

name: Divides
definition: States that one integer divides another with no remainder. a ∣ b means some integer k exists with b = a·k.

examples.explanation: Twelve equals 3 times 4, so 3 divides 12.

commonMistakes: Reading the bar as a fraction or absolute value; here it is a relation between integers.

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Grouping symbols
definition: Parentheses, square brackets and braces group parts of an expression to be evaluated first. They override the default order of operations.
reading: “open parenthesis… close parenthesis”, naming each symbol.

examples.explanation: The grouped sum is computed before multiplying.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Interval notation
definition: Describes a continuous range of numbers. Square brackets include the endpoint; round parentheses exclude it. Infinity always takes a round parenthesis.

examples.explanation: All x with 2 ≤ x < 5: 2 included, 5 excluded.
All numbers up to and including 3.

commonMistakes: Writing [2, ∞]; infinity is not a number and always takes a parenthesis.

sources.label: OpenStax College Algebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Overline (repeating decimal)
definition: A bar over digits marks them as repeating forever in a decimal expansion. In statistics the same bar on x denotes a sample mean instead — context decides.

examples.explanation: The digit 3 repeats forever: 0.333….

contexts.meaning: Repeating digits in a decimal expansion.
Sample mean of observed x values.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Scientific notation
definition: Writes very large or small numbers as a coefficient times a power of ten, with the coefficient usually between 1 and 10.

examples.explanation: Move the decimal point 4 places right.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Mixed number
definition: Writes a whole number together with a proper fraction, meaning their sum. The juxtaposition means addition here, not multiplication.

examples.explanation: Two and a half equals five halves.

commonMistakes: Reading 2½ as 2 times ½; in mixed numbers the juxtaposition means plus.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Asymptotically equal (tilde)
definition: States that two quantities become relatively equal in some limit: their ratio tends to 1. Weaker than ≈ in that it describes growth, not closeness.

examples.explanation: Stirling's formula: the ratio of the sides tends to 1 as n grows.

sources.label: NIST Digital Library of Mathematical Functions, ch. 2
sources.license: NIST DLMF; see site for citing guidance; consulted, original wording

sources.label: Unicode Mathematical Operators code chart
sources.license: Unicode License Agreement; glyph identity

name: Continued fraction
definition: Writes a number as a tower of fractions: [a₀; a₁, a₂, …] means a₀ + 1/(a₁ + 1/(a₂ + …)). Cutting the tower off gives convergents: exceptionally good rational approximations.

examples.explanation: The simple continued fraction of pi begins 3; 7, 15, 1, 292.
Stopping after the 7 gives the familiar 22/7 approximation.

sources.label: MathWorld, Pi Continued Fraction
sources.license: © Wolfram Research (MathWorld); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

sources.label: Wikibooks Subject:Mathematics
sources.license: CC BY-SA (site footer); consulted, original wording

name: Irrational numbers
definition: Real numbers that are not ratios of integers: their decimals never terminate or repeat. Square roots of non-square integers, π and e are irrational.

examples.explanation: No fraction squares to 2 (classic proof by contradiction: a lowest-terms p/q would force both even).

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Absolute and relative error
definition: Absolute error is |true − approximate|; relative error divides by the true size, measuring error in context. A 1 cm miss on a pencil versus a bridge are different stories the relative error tells.

examples.explanation: Absolute miss about 0.0016; relative miss about 0.05%.

sources.label: OpenStax Prealgebra 2e
sources.license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (openstax.org footer); consulted as reference, original wording, no text reused

name: Trapezoid rule
definition: Approximates a definite integral with trapezoids instead of rectangles: average the endpoint heights on each slice. Exact for linear functions; the error shrinks quadratically as slices narrow.

examples.explanation: For ∫₀¹x²dx the single trapezoid gives 0.5 against the exact 1/3 — an overestimate, as convexity predicts.
